blocks.h2: Basement Flooding in Joliet Homes
blocks.intro: Joliet's older and newer neighborhoods flood for different reasons.

items.body: Older areas typically have combined sewers. In heavy rain they fill, and water comes up through floor drains. A backflow valve or an [overhead sewer system](/joliet/overhead-sewer-systems) is the usual fix.
Homes built in the 1990s and 2000s mostly have separate sewers. Their wet basements usually come from groundwater and a [sump pump](/joliet/sump-pumps) that couldn't keep up.
Stone and block foundations in century-old homes let water seep through more easily. Waterproofing and drainage help.

blocks.h2: Basement Waterproofing
bodies: Waterproofing is the fix when groundwater comes through the foundation, not up a drain. Look for damp walls, water where the wall meets the floor, white chalky deposits and puddles after rain without any drain backing up. Older stone and block foundations in Joliet are especially prone to seepage.

Interior drain tile and a [sump pump](/joliet/sump-pumps) work together: the tile collects the water and the pump sends it outside. Before recommending anything, we confirm the water is coming through the foundation, not from a leak or a sewer backup.

blocks.h2: What Does a Catch Basin Do?
blocks.body: A catch basin is a buried box with a grate, set at a low point in the yard, driveway or alley. Runoff flows in, sand and leaves settle in the bottom, and the water leaves through an outlet pipe. When the bottom fills, debris reaches the outlet and the water backs up. We clean basins, clear the outlet pipe and repair basins that have cracked, sunk or crumbled.

items.q: Is a catch basin the same as a French drain?
items.preview: No. A catch basin collects surface water at a low spot. A French drain is a gravel trench.
items.answer: No. A catch basin collects surface water at one low point and sends it out through a pipe. A French drain is a gravel-filled trench with a perforated pipe. We clean and repair catch basins and their outlet pipes.

blocks.h2: When to Call for Drain Cleaning
blocks.body: Call when plunging doesn't work, when a drain clogs again within a few weeks or when you smell sewer gas. Notice where it happens. One slow sink is a local clog. A floor drain that gurgles when the washer drains, or a tub that backs up when the toilet flushes, means the main line is involved and needs [sewer rodding](/joliet/sewer-rodding).

img.alt: Illustration of common signs a drain needs professional cleaning

blocks.h2: Clogged Drain Repair in Joliet
bodies: Most clogs come from the usual suspects: hair and soap in the bathroom, grease and food in the kitchen, lint in the laundry. We clear them with a cable sized for the pipe and show you what came out.

In Joliet, the water itself plays a part. The city's well water is naturally high in minerals, and over the years scale builds up inside drains, especially old cast iron ones. Rough, scaled pipe catches hair and grease faster. If a drain keeps clogging, [hydro jetting](/joliet/hydro-jetting) clears the scale and the buildup together.

blocks.h2: Kitchen Sink Drain Unclogging
bodies: Kitchen sinks clog a little more every day. Grease cools and hardens in the pipe, and food and soap stick to it. One day the sink just won't drain.

blocks.h2: Why Drains Clog in Joliet Homes
blocks.intro: Joliet homes range from the 1800s to today, and their drains clog for different reasons.

items.body: In homes built before 1940, cast iron drains have had a century to rust and scale inside. They clog more often and need gentler handling.
Joliet's well water is naturally rich in minerals. Scale on fixtures is the visible part. The same buildup happens inside drains over the years.
If several drains back up together, the problem is the main line. In older neighborhoods, roots in clay laterals are a common cause. That's [sewer drain clearing](#sewer-drain-clearing).

blocks.h2: Sewer Drain Clearing

blocks.body: Fixtures in a basement often sit lower than the sewer line leaving the house, so gravity can't carry their wastewater out. Instead, they drain into a sealed basin. items.q: Repair or replace my garbage disposal?
items.preview: Jams and loose connections are repairs. A leaking body or dead motor means a new unit.

items.q: What can't go down a disposal?
items.preview: Grease, bones, fibrous scraps, coffee grounds and eggshells.
items.answer: Grease and oil, bones, fibrous scraps like celery and corn husks, coffee grounds, eggshells, rice and pasta. They jam the unit or build up in the drain.

items.q: How long do disposals last?
items.preview: Often around 8 to 15 years.
items.answer: Many last around 8 to 15 years, depending on the model and use. Frequent jams, leaks and louder grinding mean it's near the end.

items.q: Why does my disposal smell even when it works?
items.preview: Food trapped under the splash guard and in the drain line.
items.answer: Food gets trapped under the rubber splash guard and in the drain below. Run cold water for 15 to 20 seconds after each use, and grind a few ice cubes now and then. A smell that keeps coming back often means the drain line itself needs cleaning.

blocks.h2: Joliet Gas Fireplace Not Working Right?
blocks.intro: These are the calls we get most once the weather turns:

tiles.body: You hear the igniter click, but nothing lights. A clogged pilot orifice or a weak igniter is the usual cause after a summer off.
The flame comes on and drops out a minute later. The thermocouple or thermopile can't hold the gas valve open anymore.
A tall yellow or orange flame and dark glass point to a dirty burner, shifted logs or a vent that isn't drawing well.
Dead batteries are the easy answer. If new ones don't help, the receiver or switch wiring has failed.
Leave the house first. Call Nicor Gas or 911 from outside, then call us once they clear it.

blocks.h2: Gas Fireplace Repair, Cleaning and Yearly Service
blocks.intro: One visit covers the gas supply, the burner and the vent.

blocks.h2: From Old Masonry to New Direct-Vent: Joliet Fireplaces
blocks.intro: Joliet's housing spans more than a century, and so do its fireplaces. What we check depends a lot on when the house was built.

items.body: In the Upper Bluff and other neighborhoods near downtown, many brick fireplaces were built for wood and fitted with gas logs later. The damper has to stay open, the flue has to be clear and the gas connection has to be tight. We check all three.
Ranch homes from the 1950s and 1960s often got a gas insert in the old fireplace. Inserts vent through a liner in the chimney, and a loose or damaged liner can push exhaust back into the room.

items.q: My fireplace worked last winter. Why won't it light now?
items.preview: Dust, spider webs and debris in the pilot over summer are the usual cause.
items.answer: Over the warm months, dust and even spider webs collect in the pilot tube and burner ports. The pilot can't get enough gas to light or stay lit. A cleaning usually fixes it. If it doesn't, the thermocouple or thermopile is the next suspect.

items.q: Can gas logs go in my old wood-burning fireplace?
items.preview: Often, yes, if the chimney is sound and a gas line can reach it.
items.answer: Often, yes. The chimney needs to be in good shape and drawing well, and a gas line has to be run to the firebox. We handle the gas line and tell you if anything about the setup needs a chimney professional first.

items.q: Is it normal for my gas fireplace to smell when it first turns on?
items.preview: A brief dusty smell is normal. A gas or rotten-egg smell is not.
items.answer: A short burning-dust smell on the first fire of the season is normal and fades fast. A rotten-egg smell is not. If you smell gas, leave the house, call Nicor Gas or 911 from outside, and call us once it's safe.

items.q: How often should a gas fireplace be serviced?
items.preview: Once a year, before heating season.
items.answer: Once a year, ideally in September or October. That way a weak part shows up on a mild day instead of the first cold night.

blocks.h2: What Is Hydro Jetting?
blocks.body: Hydro jetting clears a sewer line with a high-pressure water stream, fed through the same cleanout access point used for rodding. A specialized nozzle sprays water in every direction as it moves through the pipe, scouring grease, scale, and roots off the entire pipe wall instead of just cutting a path through the middle. It's the fix for buildup that keeps coming back after rodding, or for roots that have worked into the pipe joints. Rodding opens the line back up. Hydro jetting cleans it.

tiles.body: Once is enough to look for a permanent fix.

blocks.h2: How an Overhead Sewer System Works
blocks.body: Most basement drains run by gravity to a sewer line that leaves the house below the floor. When the sewer outside fills, that same path lets water flow back in. An overhead system changes the route. Basement drains empty into a sealed pit, an [ejector pump](/joliet/ejector-pump) lifts the wastewater up to a line near the ceiling, and a check valve stops it from flowing back. Gravity carries it out to the sewer from there, the same way your upstairs drains work.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewers and Joliet Basements
blocks.intro: Overhead sewers make the most sense where storm water and sewage share the same pipes.

items.body: Joliet's older neighborhoods typically have combined sewers. In heavy rain, they can fill to the level of a basement floor drain.
Homes from the late 1800s and early 1900s often have basements and drains sitting low relative to the sewer. That makes them more exposed to backups.
We camera your line before recommending a conversion. If roots or a crack are the real cause, a [sewer repair](/joliet/sewer-repair) may be enough.

blocks.body: A tankless heater fires up only when a hot tap opens. Water flows through a heat exchanger, gets heated on the spot and goes straight to the fixture, so there's no tank to run dry. The unit has to be sized for every hot tap you run at once, and it needs the gas supply, venting or electrical service to match. In hard water, the heat exchanger also needs regular descaling to keep working at full output.

blocks.h2: What Is Trenchless Sewer Repair?
blocks.body: Trenchless sewer repair, also called no-dig sewer repair, fixes a damaged pipe without digging a trench along its full length. Instead of opening up your yard from the house to the street, we work through one or two access points and repair the pipe from the inside or replace it in place. There are two main methods: cured-in-place pipe (CIPP) lining and pipe bursting. Both fix the line underground, so what's above it stays untouched.

Joliet's water report lists water softener regeneration as a likely source of sodium in the water. A softener cuts scale but makes the anode rod work harder, so we check it.

items.h3: Lake Michigan Won't Undo the Buildup
items.body: The city expects Lake Michigan water to reach your tap in 2030, with lower hardness. The sediment already in your tank stays there until someone flushes it.

blocks.h2: Residential Water Heater Service
bodies: We service every kind of water heater found in Joliet homes: gas and electric tanks, power-vent units and tankless heaters, from century-old basements near downtown to utility rooms in west side subdivisions.

Not sure what you have? The label on the tank shows the fuel, the capacity and the manufacture date. Read it to us when you call. Ready for a new one? See [water heater installation](/joliet/water-heater-installation).

blocks.h2: Water Heater Maintenance and Flushing
bodies: In Joliet, flushing isn't optional maintenance. Mineral-heavy well water builds sediment faster than lake water does. A flush drains it out, and we also check the anode rod, the relief valve and the burner or elements while we're there.

Most manufacturers recommend flushing about once a year. With Joliet's water, homes without a softener may want to stay right on that schedule. Tankless units need regular descaling. If your heater has never been flushed, start there.

blocks.h2: Water Heater Questions From Joliet Homeowners

items.q: Is Joliet's well water bad for water heaters?
items.preview: It's hard on them. Minerals build up as sediment, so flushing matters more here.
items.answer: It's hard on them. Joliet's well water is naturally rich in minerals, and they settle in the tank as sediment. That makes the heater work harder and wear out sooner. A yearly flush, and in many homes a softener, helps it last.

items.q: Should I repair or replace my water heater?
items.preview: A leaking tank means replace. A failed part on a younger heater is usually a repair.
items.answer: If the tank is leaking, it needs replacing. If a part failed and the heater is under about 8 years old, a repair usually makes sense. We'll tell you if the repair costs too much of a new heater to be worth it.

items.q: Will switching to Lake Michigan water help my water heater?
items.preview: Going forward, yes. It won't remove the sediment already in the tank.
items.answer: Going forward, it should help, since the new supply is expected to have lower hardness. But the sediment and scale already in your tank won't leave on their own. Flush the heater, or replace it if it's near the end.
